Use a.m. or p.m. when the part of the day is unclear. Noon is midday; midnight is the start of a new day in date-based schedules. Include the date and time zone for an international meeting. Confirm rather than guess.

cards.label: PAST THE HOUR
cards.example: a quarter past nine

cards.label: BEFORE THE HOUR
cards.example: a quarter to ten

cards.label: CONFIRM
cards.example: Is that 9 a.m. Tokyo time?
cards.note: Clarify the time zone and part of day.

checks.prompt: Which time is half past two?

options.feedback: Half past means thirty minutes after the hour.
Half past means 30 minutes after the hour, not 15.
Half past two is 30 minutes after two, not before it.

checks.prompt: Which time is a quarter to six?

options.feedback: It is fifteen minutes before six.
6:45 is a quarter to seven, not six.
A quarter to six is 15 minutes before six; 6:15 is a quarter past.

checks.prompt: What should you clarify in Let’s meet at eight if you are in different countries?

options.text: The date, a.m. or p.m., and time zone.
options.feedback: A complete appointment avoids assumptions.

options.text: Only whether eight is written as a digit or a word.
options.feedback: The possible confusion is the actual date and time zone, not the spelling.

options.text: Only the length of the meeting.
options.feedback: Duration does not clarify when the meeting starts.

application.prompt: Which message gives an exact appointment date and time and asks about the time zone?

options.text: Let’s meet soon. Is that London time?
options.feedback: Soon does not give the required date and clock time.

options.text: Let’s meet on 12 September at 10 a.m. Is that London time?
options.feedback: It includes the date, clock time, a.m., and a time-zone check.

options.text: Let’s meet on 12 September at ten. I will see you then.
options.feedback: Ten leaves a.m./p.m. unclear, and no time zone is checked.

concepts.title: Even if and even though
concepts.goal: Distinguish a condition from an accepted fact.
rules: Even though introduces a fact accepted in the sentence: Even though it was raining, we walked. Even if introduces a condition or possibility that does not change the result: Even if it rains, we will walk.

The if clause does not assert that the condition is true. It can refer to a possibility or something already known in context; its job is conditional. For a likely future condition, normally use present tense after if rather than will.

cards.label: ACCEPTED FACT
cards.example: Even though I was tired, I stayed.
cards.note: The speaker says they were tired.

cards.label: CONDITION
cards.example: Even if I am tired, I will stay.
cards.note: The plan holds whether or not I am tired.

cards.label: CONTRAST
cards.example: It was expensive, but I bought it.
cards.note: But can express a simpler contrast.

checks.prompt: Which asserts rain occurred: Even if it rained / Even though it rained?

options.text: Both phrases assert that it rained.
options.feedback: Even if can discuss a condition without asserting it happened.

options.text: Even if it rained.
options.feedback: Even if presents a condition; even though presents a conceded fact.

options.text: Even though it rained.
options.feedback: Even though presents the rain as a fact.

checks.prompt: Complete: Even if she ___ late, we will wait. (arrive)

options.text: arriving
options.feedback: The clause needs a finite verb: she arrives.

options.text: arrives
options.feedback: Use present simple for this future condition.

options.text: arrive
options.feedback: She takes arrives in this present-simple conditional clause.

checks.prompt: Does Even if the shop is closed, I will go prove it is closed?

options.text: No. It proves the shop is open.
options.feedback: The sentence does not establish whether the shop is open or closed.

options.text: No. The closure is treated as a condition.
options.feedback: The sentence does not establish its truth.

options.text: Yes. Even if asserts that the shop is closed.
options.feedback: Even if presents the closure as a condition, not an established fact.

application.prompt: The weather may be bad, but you will go to class either way. Which sentence expresses that plan?

options.text: Even if the weather is bad, I will go to class.
options.feedback: Even if presents a possible difficulty that will not change the plan.

options.text: Even though the weather is bad, I will go to class.
options.feedback: Even though presents bad weather as a fact; the prompt gives it as a possibility.

options.text: If the weather is bad, I will stay home.
options.feedback: This changes the plan when the weather is bad.

concepts.title: Care about and care for
concepts.goal: Say what matters to you and who you look after.
rules: Care about commonly means consider important: I care about the environment. Care for can mean look after: She cares for her father. Take care of also means look after or deal with.

Care for can mean like or want in some contexts: I do not care for this music; Would you care for some tea? These uses are often more formal. I do not care can sound dismissive, so choose a clearer phrase when you simply have no preference.

cards.label: IMPORTANCE
cards.example: I care about the result.
cards.note: The result matters to me.

cards.label: LOOK AFTER
cards.example: I care for my grandmother.
cards.note: I help look after her.

cards.label: NO PREFERENCE
cards.example: Either time works for me.
cards.note: A considerate alternative to I do not care.

checks.prompt: Choose the phrase that expresses concern for an issue: We care ___ clean water.

options.text: about
options.feedback: This expresses importance or concern.

options.text: of
options.feedback: Care about introduces a concern or issue; care of does not fit this verb phrase.

options.text: to
options.feedback: Care to normally takes a verb, as in care to join, not the noun phrase clean water.

checks.prompt: He cares for his elderly neighbor by cooking meals and helping with daily tasks. What does cares for mean here?

options.text: Look after.
options.feedback: The context describes providing care.

options.text: Ask the neighbor for advice.
options.feedback: The phrase describes giving care, not seeking advice.

options.text: Have no preference about.
options.feedback: Cares for his elderly neighbor here means looks after the neighbor.

checks.prompt: Choose an alternative to I do not care when either restaurant is fine.

options.text: Either restaurant is fine with me.
options.feedback: This states a preference without sounding dismissive.

options.text: Neither restaurant is acceptable.
options.feedback: This rejects both restaurants; the intended meaning accepts either.

options.text: I strongly prefer the first restaurant.
options.feedback: This expresses a preference, whereas the intended meaning is no preference.

application.prompt: Punctuality matters to you, but you accept either cafe. Which pair communicates both points?

options.text: I care about arriving on time. Neither cafe is acceptable.
options.feedback: Neither rejects both cafes, contrary to the stated preference.

options.text: I care about arriving on time. Either cafe works for me.
options.feedback: Care about expresses the concern; either cafe accepts both options.

options.text: I do not care about arriving on time. Either cafe works for me.
options.feedback: This denies the stated importance of punctuality.

concepts.title: Success, succeed, successful, successfully
concepts.goal: Use the correct member of a word family.
rules: Success is a noun: The event was a success. Succeed is a verb: We succeeded. Successful is an adjective: The event was successful. Successfully is an adverb: We completed it successfully.

Use succeed in + -ing for achieving an action: succeed in finding a solution. Not every noun use needs an article: hard work can contribute to success. Describe what the success means instead of relying only on a positive label.

cards.label: NOUN
cards.example: The event was a success.
cards.note: A success names a successful event.

cards.label: VERB
cards.example: We succeeded in finding a room.
cards.note: In is followed by an -ing form.

cards.label: ADVERB
cards.example: We booked the room successfully.
cards.note: Successfully modifies booked.

checks.prompt: Complete: The project was ___ . (success / successful)

options.text: successful
options.feedback: An adjective describes the project.

options.text: successfully
options.feedback: Successfully is an adverb; was needs successful or a success here.

options.text: success
options.feedback: Without an article, this position needs successful; a success is another valid pattern.

checks.prompt: Complete: We succeeded in ___ the problem. (solve)

options.text: solve
options.feedback: After in, use the -ing form solving.

options.text: to solve
options.feedback: Use succeeded in solving, not in to solve.

options.text: solving
options.feedback: Use -ing after in.

checks.prompt: Choose the adverb: success / successful / successfully

options.text: successfully
options.feedback: The adverb can describe how an action was completed.

options.text: success
options.feedback: Success is a noun, not an adverb.

options.text: successful
options.feedback: Successful is an adjective; successfully is the adverb.

application.prompt: Which pair uses the success word family correctly to describe an achievement?

options.text: We successfully organized the meeting. It was a success because everyone could join.
options.feedback: Successfully modifies organized; a success is a noun phrase.

options.text: We successful organized the meeting. It was a success.
options.feedback: Use the adverb successfully to modify organized.

options.text: We successfully organized the meeting. It was a successfully.
options.feedback: After a, use the noun success rather than the adverb.

concepts.title: Could and was able to
concepts.goal: Distinguish past ability from a particular achievement.
rules: Could commonly describes a general past ability: At ten, I could swim. For an actual achievement on one particular occasion, was/were able to or managed to is usually clearer: We were able to catch the last train.

The distinction is not absolute. Could is natural for particular past perceptions or mental states: I could hear music. Could not can describe a specific failure: I could not open the door. Could also expresses possibility and polite requests in other contexts.

cards.label: GENERAL ABILITY
cards.example: I could read when I was five.
cards.note: A skill at a past age.

cards.label: ACHIEVEMENT
cards.example: We managed to finish before noon.
cards.note: A successful result on an occasion.

cards.label: PERCEPTION
cards.example: I could hear the train coming.
cards.note: A natural use for a particular past perception.

checks.prompt: Choose for a skill you had as a child: When I was seven, I ___ swim.

options.text: will
options.feedback: Will refers to the future here. At seven describes an ability in childhood, so use could.

options.text: can
options.feedback: Can describes present ability. This sentence describes a childhood skill in the past.

options.text: could
options.feedback: Could describes a general past ability. Was able to can also express past ability.

checks.prompt: Choose the phrase that reports an actual success: Yesterday, we ___ get the last two tickets.

options.text: tried to
options.feedback: Tried to reports the attempt, not whether it succeeded. Managed to states the successful result.

options.text: hoped to
options.feedback: Hoped to tells us what they wanted, but it does not say they succeeded in getting the tickets.

options.text: managed to
options.feedback: Managed to reports an actual successful result. Were able to can also express that meaning.

checks.prompt: Is I could hear a bell outside natural?

options.text: Yes. Could commonly occurs with perception verbs.
options.feedback: Do not apply the achievement rule to every past use.

options.text: No. Hear must always be in a continuous form.
options.feedback: Could hear is a normal way to describe a past perception.

options.text: No. Could can only describe general skills.
options.feedback: Could is also natural with perception verbs such as hear.

application.prompt: Which pair reports a general childhood ability and then a specific successful result yesterday?

options.text: I could cycle when I was young. Yesterday I managed to repair a flat tire.
options.feedback: Could describes the past skill; managed to reports the successful repair.

options.text: I will cycle when I was young. Yesterday I managed to repair a flat tire.
options.feedback: Will does not express the childhood ability in the past.

options.text: I could cycle when I was young. Yesterday I could have repaired a flat tire, but I did not.
options.feedback: The second sentence explicitly says the repair was not done, so it is not a successful result.

concepts.title: Speak, talk, say, and tell
concepts.goal: Choose a verb that fits the message and listener.
rules: Say focuses on the words or message: She said hello; she said that she was busy. Tell commonly names the listener directly: She told me that she was busy. Use say something to someone, not say someone something.

Speak and talk often overlap for conversation. Speak is common with languages: speak Arabic. Talk about introduces a topic. Learn common exceptions as phrases: tell a story, tell the truth, speak to someone, talk to or with someone.

cards.label: MESSAGE
cards.example: She said the meeting was canceled.
cards.note: The focus is the message.

cards.label: LISTENER
cards.example: She told me the meeting was canceled.
cards.note: Me identifies the listener.

cards.label: TOPIC
cards.example: We talked about the schedule.
cards.note: About introduces the topic.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: She said me the answer.

options.text: She said me to the answer.
options.feedback: Say does not take a person directly in this pattern. Use She told me the answer.

options.text: She told to me the answer.
options.feedback: Tell takes the recipient directly here: told me the answer.

options.text: She told me the answer.
options.feedback: Alternatively: She said the answer to me.

checks.prompt: Complete: Do you ___ Korean?

options.text: speak
options.feedback: Speak is the usual verb for language ability.

options.text: say
options.feedback: Speak is used for knowing or using a language.

options.text: tell
options.feedback: Tell normally communicates a message; speak Korean names a language ability.

checks.prompt: Does tell always need a listener?

options.text: No. Tell can never name a listener.
options.feedback: Tell me and tell the team are normal patterns.

options.text: Yes. Every use must name a listener.
options.feedback: Expressions such as tell the truth do not need an explicit listener.

options.text: No. Common phrases include tell a story and tell the truth.
options.feedback: Learn the whole phrase with its meaning.

application.prompt: Your colleague gave you a message about a new room. Which report is grammatical and names the recipient?

options.text: My colleague said me that the room had changed.
options.feedback: Say does not take me directly in this pattern; use told me or said to me.

options.text: My colleague told to me that the room had changed.
options.feedback: Tell takes the recipient directly here: told me.

options.text: My colleague told me that the room had changed.
options.feedback: Told me names the recipient and introduces the reported message.

concepts.title: Most and almost
concepts.goal: Distinguish a majority from something nearly true.
rules: Most before a plural or uncountable noun means the majority or greatest part: most students, most water. Use most of before a determiner or pronoun: most of the students; most of them.

Almost means nearly: almost ready, almost all, almost everyone. It does not normally directly modify a plural noun to mean the majority: say most people or almost all people, depending on your meaning. Almost all is stronger than most.

cards.label: MAJORITY
cards.example: Most students came.
cards.note: More than half came; the precise number is unstated.

cards.label: NEARLY EVERYONE
cards.example: Almost all the students came.
cards.note: Very few were absent.

cards.label: NEARLY A STATE
cards.example: The room is almost ready.
cards.note: Some preparation remains.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: Almost people arrived on time.

options.text: Most people arrived on time.
options.feedback: If nearly everyone arrived on time, use Almost all the people instead.

options.text: Most people almosts arrived on time.
options.feedback: Almost does not take an -s ending, and the intended claim is about most people.

options.text: Almost of the people arrived on time.
options.feedback: Use most of the people or almost all of the people, not almost of.

checks.prompt: Complete: Most ___ them agreed.

options.text: to
options.feedback: Use of between most and an object pronoun such as them.

options.text: from
options.feedback: Most of them identifies a proportion of that group.

options.text: of
options.feedback: Use of before a pronoun such as them.

checks.prompt: Which suggests a larger share: most / almost all?

options.text: Neither; both mean exactly half.
options.feedback: Most means more than half and almost all means nearly everyone or everything.

options.text: most
options.feedback: Most means a majority; almost all normally suggests close to the whole group.

options.text: almost all
options.feedback: It means nearly the entire group.

application.prompt: Which pair correctly describes a majority of classmates and a nearly finished project?

options.text: Most of my classmates walk to school. Our project is almost finished.
options.feedback: Most of refers to a proportion of the group; almost means nearly.

options.text: Almost my classmates walk to school. Our project is almost finished.
options.feedback: Use most of my classmates or almost all of my classmates.

options.text: Most of my classmates walk to school. Our project is most finished.
options.feedback: Use almost finished to mean nearly complete.

concepts.title: Affect and effect
concepts.goal: Describe an influence and its result.
rules: Affect is usually a verb meaning influence: The noise affected my sleep. Effect is usually a noun meaning a result or influence: The noise had an effect on my sleep.

There are less common meanings: effect can be a formal verb meaning bring about, as in effect change; affect can be a specialist noun about outward emotional expression. Start with the common patterns, but do not treat the spelling distinction as exceptionless. A causal claim still needs evidence.

cards.label: VERB
cards.example: The delay affected our plans.
cards.note: Affected tells what the delay did.

cards.label: NOUN
cards.example: The delay had an effect on our plans.
cards.note: Effect is the noun after an.

cards.label: CAUTIOUS CLAIM
cards.example: The delay may affect our plans.
cards.note: May preserves uncertainty.

checks.prompt: Choose the verb meaning influence: The weather can ___ travel.

options.text: affect
options.feedback: A verb is needed after can.

options.text: affection
options.feedback: Affection is a noun meaning fondness, not the verb influence.

options.text: effect
options.feedback: The usual verb meaning influence is affect; effect as a verb means bring about.

checks.prompt: Choose the noun meaning result: What ___ did the change have?

options.text: affect
options.feedback: This sentence needs the noun effect meaning result or influence.

options.text: effective
options.feedback: Effective is an adjective; the question asks what effect the change had.

options.text: effect
options.feedback: This question asks about the result as a noun.

checks.prompt: Is effect never a verb?

options.text: No. Effect change means bring change about.
options.feedback: That formal use is less common than the noun.

options.text: No. As a verb, effect always means notice.
options.feedback: The verb effect means bring about, not notice.

options.text: Yes. Effect is only ever a noun.
options.feedback: Effect can be a formal verb meaning bring about, as in effect change.

application.prompt: The timetable’s influence on your journey is uncertain. Which sentence preserves that uncertainty?

options.text: The new timetable may affect my journey to work.
options.feedback: May keeps the outcome possible rather than certain, and affect means influence.

options.text: The new timetable will definitely shorten my journey to work.
options.feedback: This asserts a particular outcome and certainty not provided in the prompt.

options.text: The new timetable may affection my journey to work.
options.feedback: Affection is a noun, not the verb needed after may.

concepts.title: Look, watch, hear, and listen
concepts.goal: Describe attention and perception.
rules: Look at directs visual attention toward something. Watch usually involves attention over time, often to something changing or moving. Hear describes receiving sound; listen emphasizes paying attention to it.

Use to before the object of listen: listen to music. Hear does not need to before its object. The attention distinction is useful but not absolute: hear a speaker can also mean attend a talk. Learn familiar activity phrases such as watch television and look at a photo.

cards.label: DIRECT ATTENTION
cards.example: Look at this photo.
cards.note: Turn your attention to it.

cards.label: OVER TIME
cards.example: We watched the match.
cards.note: Follow an event as it develops.

cards.label: SOUND
cards.example: I heard music and stopped to listen to it.
cards.note: The sound was perceived, then attended to.

checks.prompt: Complete: Please listen ___ the announcement.

options.text: at
options.feedback: Listen takes to before the thing you intentionally attend to.

options.text: to
options.feedback: Listen takes to before the object.

options.text: for to
options.feedback: Use listen to the announcement without for.

checks.prompt: Choose the verb for viewing the game as it happened: We ___ the game.

options.text: watched
options.feedback: Watch is natural for following a game.

options.text: listened
options.feedback: Listen would need to and would describe attending to sound rather than watching.

options.text: looked
options.feedback: With the game as the direct object, watch fits. Look would need at.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: I heard to a loud noise.

options.text: I listened a loud noise.
options.feedback: Listen needs to; hear takes its object directly.

options.text: I heard at a loud noise.
options.feedback: Hear takes a loud noise directly, without at.

options.text: I heard a loud noise.
options.feedback: Hear takes the object directly.

application.prompt: You first noticed a voice, then paid attention to an announcement. Which pair fits?

options.text: I heard a voice outside. I listened the announcement.
options.feedback: Listen needs to before the object.

options.text: I heard a voice outside. I listened to the announcement.
options.feedback: Heard describes noticing sound; listened to describes deliberate attention.

options.text: I heard to a voice outside. I listened to the announcement.
options.feedback: Hear takes its object directly, without to.

concepts.title: So and such
concepts.goal: Add emphasis using the right sentence pattern.
rules: Use so before an adjective or adverb: so helpful, so quickly. Use such before a noun phrase: such a helpful person, such helpful people. With a singular countable noun, keep a or an.

Use so with many, much, few, and little when these describe quantities: so many books, so little time. A following that clause can give a result: It was so noisy that I left. Emphasis is a choice, not a factual measurement.

cards.label: ADJECTIVE
cards.example: The guide was so helpful.
cards.note: So modifies helpful.

cards.label: NOUN PHRASE
cards.example: She was such a helpful guide.
cards.note: Such introduces the noun phrase.

cards.label: QUANTITY
cards.example: There were so many questions.
cards.note: So combines with many.

checks.prompt: Complete: It was ___ a useful lesson.

options.text: such as
options.feedback: Such as introduces examples, not this degree expression.

options.text: so
options.feedback: Use such before a noun phrase with a: such a useful lesson.

options.text: such
options.feedback: A useful lesson is a noun phrase.

checks.prompt: Complete: The room was ___ quiet.

options.text: such
options.feedback: Before the adjective quiet alone, use so.

options.text: such a
options.feedback: Such a needs a following noun phrase, such as such a quiet room.

options.text: so
options.feedback: Quiet is an adjective without a following noun.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: We had such much work.

options.text: We had such many work.
options.feedback: The pattern is so much work.

options.text: We had so much work.
options.feedback: Use so before the quantity word much.

options.text: We had so many work.
options.feedback: Work is uncountable in this meaning, so use much rather than many.

application.prompt: Which sentence uses so correctly and gives the result of clear instructions?

options.text: The instructions were so clearly that I finished without help.
options.feedback: Were needs the adjective clear for this description, not the adverb clearly.

options.text: The instructions were so clear that I finished without help.
options.feedback: So modifies the adjective clear; that introduces the result.

options.text: The instructions were such clear that I finished without help.
options.feedback: Use so before clear alone, or such clear instructions with a noun.

concepts.title: Refuse and reject
concepts.goal: Decline an action or turn down an offer.
rules: Refuse can take to + verb: I refused to sign. It can also take an offer or request: refuse an invitation. Reject commonly takes a noun naming something not accepted: reject a proposal, reject an application.

Do not use reject to do for declining an action. Either verb can sound strong depending on context. Decline is often a courteous choice for an invitation. State a reason or an alternative when it helps the conversation, without inventing one.

cards.label: ACTION
cards.example: She refused to sign the form.
cards.note: Refuse takes a to-infinitive.

cards.label: PROPOSAL
cards.example: They rejected the proposal.
cards.note: Reject takes the proposal as its object.

cards.label: INVITATION
cards.example: Thank you, but I must decline.
cards.note: A courteous way to turn down an invitation.

checks.prompt: Complete: He refused ___ answer.

options.text: from
options.feedback: Use refused to answer, not refused from answer.

options.text: for
options.feedback: Refuse takes a to-infinitive for the action: refused to answer.

options.text: to
options.feedback: Use refuse to do something.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: They rejected to meet us.

options.text: They refused meet us.
options.feedback: Refuse needs to before the infinitive: refused to meet.

options.text: They rejected meeting to us.
options.feedback: This is not a correct replacement for the stated decision not to meet.

options.text: They refused to meet us.
options.feedback: Reject does not take this to-infinitive pattern.

checks.prompt: Can refuse take a noun?

options.text: No. Refuse must always take a to-infinitive.
options.feedback: Refuse can take a noun, such as help or an invitation.

options.text: Yes: refuse an invitation or refuse help.
options.feedback: Its patterns are broader than refuse to do.

options.text: Yes, but only the noun answer.
options.feedback: Many nouns can follow refuse, including help and an invitation.

application.prompt: You cannot attend an event and have given no reason. Which reply declines politely without inventing one?

options.text: Thank you for inviting me. I look forward to joining you.
options.feedback: This accepts the invitation rather than declining.

options.text: Thank you for inviting me, but I cannot join because I am ill.
options.feedback: The prompt does not establish illness; the reply invents a reason.

options.text: Thank you for inviting me, but I cannot join you this time.
options.feedback: This declines courteously without adding an unsupported explanation.

concepts.title: Explain an unfamiliar idea
concepts.goal: Help a listener understand a new term.
rules: Start with a familiar category, then describe the defining feature and give a concrete example. A commuter is a person who regularly travels between home and work. The example should clarify the definition, not replace it.

Adjust the detail to the listener. Ask what they already know and check understanding with a useful question. Avoid explaining one unfamiliar word through several more unfamiliar words. An analogy helps only if you also state where it differs.

cards.label: CATEGORY
cards.example: A library is a place where people can borrow books.
cards.note: Start with a familiar kind of thing.

cards.label: EXAMPLE
cards.example: You can borrow a novel and return it later.
cards.note: Make the activity concrete.

cards.label: CHECK
cards.example: How is borrowing different from buying?
cards.note: Ask about the important distinction.

checks.prompt: Which opening is clearer for a beginner: A commuter is a person ... / A commuter is an intermodal participant ...?

options.text: Both are equally easy for every beginner.
options.feedback: A simple familiar category such as person gives a beginner a clearer starting point.

options.text: A commuter is an intermodal participant ...
options.feedback: This replaces an unfamiliar word with another difficult expression.

options.text: A commuter is a person ...
options.feedback: A familiar category gives the listener a starting point.

checks.prompt: Which sentence explains borrow?

options.text: Borrow means give someone something for a time.
options.feedback: That describes lend from the owner’s perspective, not borrow from the user’s.

options.text: Borrow means use something for a time and then return it.
options.feedback: Include the temporary use and expected return.

options.text: Borrow means keep something permanently without returning it.
options.feedback: Borrowing normally involves temporary use and returning the item.

checks.prompt: Why might an example alone be insufficient?

options.text: It may not show what all uses have in common.
options.feedback: A short definition gives the general meaning.

options.text: An example always gives a complete definition.
options.feedback: An example illustrates one case and may leave the wider meaning unclear.

options.text: Definitions should never contain examples.
options.feedback: Examples can help, especially alongside a short general explanation.

application.prompt: Which explanation gives a beginner a simple category and the basic use of a delivery locker?

options.text: A delivery locker is an asynchronous fulfillment endpoint.
options.feedback: This relies on difficult technical terms and gives no simple action.

options.text: A delivery locker is a secure place to collect a package. You use a code to open its door.
options.feedback: The explanation identifies the kind of place and gives a concrete action.

options.text: A delivery locker is a place where you buy a package and choose its contents.
options.feedback: This confuses collecting a delivered package with shopping.

concepts.title: Describing trends
concepts.goal: Describe a change with its amount and time period.
rules: Use rise, increase, fall, or decrease for direction. Use remain stable for little change and fluctuate for repeated movement up and down. A number without a time period or unit can be misleading.

Distinguish rise by from rise to: from 40 to 50 is a rise by 10, ending at 50. A change from 20% to 25% is five percentage points, or a 25% relative increase. Describe the data separately from an explanation of its cause.

cards.label: START AND END
cards.example: Attendance rose from 40 to 50 in June.
cards.note: The unit is people; the period is June.

cards.label: AMOUNT
cards.example: Attendance rose by 10.
cards.note: By introduces the size of the change.

cards.label: LIMIT
cards.example: The figures rose, but the cause is unclear.
cards.note: The trend alone does not establish a cause.

checks.prompt: Attendance rose from 20 to 30. How much did it rise by?

options.text: 30 people
options.feedback: 30 is the final total. The increase is 30 minus 20.

options.text: 20 people
options.feedback: 20 is the starting total, not the amount of increase.

options.text: 10 people
options.feedback: Subtract the starting count from the ending count.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: Sales rose by 500 to 600.

options.text: Sales rose to 500 from 600.
options.feedback: This reverses the starting and finishing values and describes a fall.

options.text: Sales rose from 500 to 600.
options.feedback: From and to give the starting and ending values.

options.text: Sales rose from 500 by 600.
options.feedback: This says the increase was 600, which would give a final value of 1100.

checks.prompt: A rate rises from 10% to 12%. How many percentage points is that?

options.text: 12 percentage points
options.feedback: 12% is the final rate. Subtract 10 from 12 to find the percentage-point increase.

options.text: 2 percentage points
options.feedback: Subtract the percentages; the relative increase is 20%.

options.text: 20 percentage points
options.feedback: 20% is the relative increase from 10 to 12, not the percentage-point difference.

application.prompt: Bus use increased from 80 to 100 journeys per day in July. The cause is unknown. Which report preserves those facts?

options.text: Bus use rose by 100 journeys per day in July because fares fell.
options.feedback: The increase was 20, not 100, and the cause is invented.

options.text: Bus fares rose from 80 to 100 dollars per day in July.
options.feedback: This changes both the thing measured and its unit.

options.text: Bus use rose from 80 to 100 journeys per day in July. The reason is not yet clear.
options.feedback: The report includes the values, unit, period, and uncertainty about cause.

concepts.title: Asking for and giving advice
concepts.goal: Ask a focused question and offer a useful option.
rules: Give enough context for the listener to understand the problem. State your goal or constraint, then ask a specific question: I have ten minutes. Which route would you suggest? Advice is normally uncountable: some advice, a piece of advice.

When responding, offer an option and a reason. Could can present a possibility; should can make a stronger recommendation. Ask a clarifying question when information is missing. Acknowledge limits rather than giving confident advice on something you do not know.

cards.label: CONTEXT
cards.example: I need to reach the station by nine.
cards.note: State the goal and constraint.

cards.label: QUESTION
cards.example: Which route would you recommend?
cards.note: Ask something the listener can answer.

cards.label: OPTION + REASON
cards.example: You could take the bus because it stops nearby.
cards.note: Offer an option with a relevant reason.

checks.prompt: Choose the correction: Can you give me an advice?

options.text: Can you give me some advices?
options.feedback: Advice is normally uncountable, so do not add -s.

options.text: Can you give me some advice?
options.feedback: Advice is normally uncountable.

options.text: Can you give me a advice?
options.feedback: Advice is not normally used with a; use some advice or a piece of advice.

checks.prompt: Which question is more focused: What should I do? / Which bus goes to the station?

options.text: What should I do?
options.feedback: This gives no specific decision or goal. The bus question identifies the information needed.

options.text: Which bus goes to the station?
options.feedback: It specifies the information needed.

options.text: Both questions identify exactly the same problem.
options.feedback: Only the bus question gives a specific destination and information need.

checks.prompt: What should you do before advising if the deadline is unclear?

options.text: Assume the deadline is today.
options.feedback: An assumption can lead to unsuitable advice. Ask about the timing.

options.text: Recommend the quickest option without asking.
options.feedback: The timing affects which advice fits the person’s needs.

options.text: Ask when the person needs to finish or arrive.
options.feedback: Clarify the missing constraint.

application.prompt: A learner needs a quiet study place. Which exchange gives a relevant option with a reason?

options.text: I need a quiet place to study. You must go somewhere immediately.
options.feedback: This gives no specific option or reason and adds unsupported urgency.

options.text: I need a quiet place to study. Try the loud music bar because it has live bands.
options.feedback: The suggested reason conflicts with the need for quiet.

options.text: I need a quiet place to study. Where would you suggest? You could try the library because it has a quiet room.
options.feedback: The question gives the need; the suggestion and reason directly address quiet study.
